title: 6 Russian Words for a Country Sliding Into Authoritarianism
gist: Book excerpt from Kuznetsova and Storyev using six Russian words (vlast', byudjetniki, zona, kadyrovization, digital gulag, 'tank stuck at the circus', dna net) to map how authoritarianism consolidates, and warning that similar warning signs appear in the UK, Israel and the US. Key mechanisms: state-dependent workforces as regime infrastructure, regional testbeds for repression, and convenience-driven state super-apps that double as control tools.

insights.claim: Modern authoritarian drift is hard to recognize from inside because today's dictators speak of freedom and democracy while subjects keep world-class technology, visa-free travel and middle-class comforts.
insights.speaker: Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev
insights.so_what: Material normality is not evidence of political stability or rule-of-law safety; country-risk models should not rely on consumer indicators.
insights.quote: Today’s dictators don’t necessarily wear military uniforms. In public speeches, they talk about freedom and democracy.
insights.locator: It can be difficult to recognize

insights.claim: The Russian concept of vlast' fuses power with the state itself, which the authors argue explains why Russian politicians focus on capturing the state; a leader using supposedly apolitical agencies against opponents is a warning sign of this mindset.
insights.speaker: Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev
insights.so_what: Weaponization of regulators and neutral agencies is an early indicator of institutional capture and rising policy risk.
insights.quote: If your president is threatening to use state mechanisms and supposedly apolitical government agencies to trammel his opponents—beware.

insights.claim: Byudjetniki, people whose livelihood depends on the state (teachers, doctors, students, bureaucrats, state-company workers), are the human material of tyranny: they are coerced into pro-government rallies and support whoever promises immediate stability regardless of long-term cost.
insights.speaker: Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev
insights.so_what: The larger the state-dependent share of employment, the easier regime entrenchment; a structural variable for political-risk scoring.
insights.quote: Byudjetniki are the human material out of which tyranny is built.

insights.claim: Regional mayors and governors in Russia receive quotas for municipal workers to dispatch to pro-government rallies, and students and factory workers are threatened with expulsion or termination for not attending.
insights.speaker: Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev
insights.so_what: Illustrates the coercive machinery behind apparent popular support, which inflates perceived regime legitimacy.
insights.quote: Regional mayors and governors receive quotas for how many municipal workers should be dispatched.

insights.claim: Repressive policies are often tested in Chechnya under Ramzan Kadyrov before being rolled out across Russia; forced on-camera apologies by suspects began there and are now a favored law-enforcement practice nationwide.
insights.speaker: Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev
insights.so_what: Watch peripheral 'testbed' jurisdictions as leading indicators of future national-level repression.
insights.quote: Repressive policies are often tested in Chechnya before they are implemented elsewhere in Russia.

insights.claim: Violence tolerated in a cordoned-off zone never stays contained; the violent tactics leaders use to rise to power inevitably become a violent system of governance, as with the Bolsheviks and Italian fascists.
insights.speaker: Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev
insights.so_what: Argues against complacency when abuses appear geographically or socially limited; tail risks spread.
insights.quote: If you allow violence to exist, even if you try to contain it, it will inevitably spread and reproduce further.
insights.locator: What does this have to do

insights.claim: Because so many Russians have been imprisoned, prison (zona) norms have seeped into wider society and still serve as a benchmark for social norms, as in Soviet times.
insights.speaker: Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev
insights.so_what: Mass incarceration reshapes social norms and institutional trust over generations.
insights.quote: Because so many people have been imprisoned, the zona’s norms have seeped into society at large.

insights.claim: After a Facebook post sparked Ukraine's 2013 Maidan Revolution, the Kremlin clamped down on online speech; in 2019 parliament mandated relocating internet infrastructure into Russia, with China's Great Firewall as the model, and tested disconnection from the global internet.
insights.speaker: Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev
insights.so_what: Internet sovereignty mandates signal rising operating risk for foreign platforms and data-localization costs.
insights.quote: In 2019, Russia’s parliament mandated that physical internet infrastructure be relocated to Russia in the name of sovereignty—in other words, to make it easier to control.

insights.claim: Russia's 'digital gulag' is popular partly because it is convenient: a single state mega-app streamlines government services, two-click doctor bookings and instant bank transfers, while the same app is used to levy fines for anti-war protest and deliver draft notices.
insights.speaker: Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev
insights.so_what: State super-apps bundle convenience with surveillance; convenience drives adoption and makes the control infrastructure sticky and hard to oppose.
insights.quote: The same state-developed app that allows residents to pay their utility bills has been utilized by the Kremlin to charge fines for protesting the war in Ukraine and even to send draft notices.

insights.claim: 2022 legislation in Russia banned calling the war in Ukraine a 'war', even online, making censorship ubiquitous.
insights.speaker: Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev
insights.so_what: Speech criminalization raises legal exposure for platforms, media and employees operating in-country.

insights.claim: Authoritarian regimes look stable from outside but are internally fragile and chaotic, so crises can brew for years and erupt suddenly, as with Prigozhin's 2023 Wagner mutiny that seized Rostov-on-Don.
insights.speaker: Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev
insights.so_what: Autocracy risk is fat-tailed: low observed volatility masks discontinuous regime shocks that markets underprice.
insights.quote: The hidden paradox of authoritarianism is that while it may appear stable from the outside, inside it is fragile and chaotic.

insights.claim: Under creeping authoritarianism there is 'no rock bottom': norms are broken repeatedly and the unthinkable becomes routine, as shown by the escalation against Alexei Navalny from election ban to poisoning, jailing and death.
insights.speaker: Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev
insights.so_what: Investors should not anchor on 'they would never do X' assumptions about institutional limits in backsliding states.
insights.quote: Whenever you think you’ve reached the bottom, authoritarians invent something new beneath it. What was once unthinkable becomes routine.
insights.locator: Dna net: There is no rock bottom

insights.claim: The authors explicitly argue Russia's authoritarian warning signs have striking parallels in the United Kingdom, Israel and the United States.
insights.speaker: Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev
insights.so_what: Signals rising elite concern about democratic backsliding in core Western markets, a long-horizon governance risk.
insights.quote: But authoritarianism can spread—read closely, and you might find striking parallels to warning signs in the United Kingdom, Israel, the United States, and beyond.
